issues.item: Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
issues.explanation: For a stalking trauma profile, 'Medical Procedures' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the report. The memory items describe classic reliving/terror reactions, and the formulation shows a strong Memory → Triggers link, implying triggers should plausibly cue the stalking memory. 'Loud noises' and possibly 'happy families' can occur idiosyncratically, but a medical examination trigger is clinically disconnected from stalking unless there is additional trauma content not represented elsewhere. This makes the trigger set less coherent with the trauma type and formulation.

vignette: Samantha, a 38-year-old South Eastern Asian woman and stock broker in her late thirties, has been experiencing significant distress following an intense period of stalking that lasted several months. She is in a relationship but finds herself increasingly isolated from both her partner and colleagues due to the intrusive symptoms she experiences daily. The traumatic event began when Samantha received repeated threatening messages and phone calls from an unknown individual who knew intimate details about her life. The stalker's persistence escalated until one evening, he appeared outside her home, causing an intense panic attack. This experience left Samantha with a vivid memory that feels surreal yet terrifyingly real. She often relives the event, feeling as though it is happening all over again when she thinks about it. "The memory is so extreme," she had come to believe, "it's hard to believe it actually happened to me." This traumatic recollection has significantly impacted her daily life and professional environment. Samantha now finds herself hyper-vigilant and easily triggered by loud noises, which remind her of the sudden appearance of her stalker outside her home. These auditory triggers often occur in bustling stock exchanges where she works, causing her to withdraw into a state of fear and anxiety. "Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time," Samantha recounted during one of our sessions. The olfactory trigger of alcohol is another potent reminder of that night when she had been drinking with friends just before the incident occurred. Whenever she catches a whiff of alcohol, she finds herself reliving the moment, feeling the same overwhelming fear and helplessness as if it were happening again. This has led her to avoid social settings where alcohol is present, further isolating her from her partner and colleagues. Moreover, seeing happy families in public areas intensifies her sense of vulnerability. She often feels a deep unease when she witnesses couples or families out on the streets, reminiscent of how alone and vulnerable she felt during that night. This has caused her to avoid places where such scenes are common, further isolating herself from others. The cumulative effect of these triggers and memories has significantly impacted Samantha's ability to function at work. She often finds it difficult to concentrate during meetings or when trading stocks due to the intrusive thoughts and overwhelming emotions triggered by loud noises in the office. This decline in performance has led to conflicts with her colleagues, who have noticed a shift in her behavior but do not understand its roots. Samantha's fear of being stalked again has grown so intense that it dominates her daily life. She had come to believe that she was constantly under threat and that any loud noise could be a signal of danger. This pervasive sense of danger has made it increasingly difficult for Samantha to maintain her composure at work, causing significant distress in both her professional and personal relationships. It is these overwhelming symptoms and their debilitating consequences that have finally prompted Samantha to seek help. She is most afraid of losing control completely, unable to distinguish between the past trauma and present reality. However, she also hopes that with support, she can regain a sense of safety and normalcy in her life. "I just want to feel safe again," she expressed during our last session, "without constantly being haunted by what happened."
